extracted.intended_audience: technology transfer practitioners and those who might license trademarks in conjunction with technologies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, investigating, and registering trademarks and related marks (service marks, trade dress, domain names, certification/collective marks) primarily for technology transfer and licensing contexts under U.S. law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark definition and function
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark or brand name is any word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination which is adopted and used in commerce by a manufacturer or business person; to identify that person’s goods or products; to distinguish those goods from goods manufactured or sold by another; and to indicate the source of the identified goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of what may function as a mark include: word or group of words (slogan), logo/symbol/pictorial representation/design, combination of words plus symbol, numerals/letters, shape of a container or packaging (Coke bottle), color (orange for The Home Depot), sound (lion roar for MGM), and scent (U.S. Trademark Registration No. 1,639,128 for a ‘high impact, fresh flower fragrance reminiscent of plumeria blossoms’). The core functional test is use in commerce to identify source and distinguish goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service mark (vs trademark)
rubrics_metrics.description: A service mark is similar to a trademark, however, it is used in the sale or advertising of services rather than goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service marks are afforded the same legal protection as trademarks and are registerable in the same manner and with the same effect. Examples: McDonald’s and Office Depot as service marks identifying services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade name limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally, the name of a business entity is not registerable unless it is used as a trademark or service mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trade name is usually identified by Company/Co., Corp./Inc., or Ltd. Trade-name infringement is actionable under federal and state laws. Example contrast: McDonald’s Corp. (trade name) v. McDonald’s restaurants (service mark). Incorporation or state assumed-name filing alone does not automatically give the right to use the name as a mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade dress protectability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover for trade-dress infringement, a plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) its trade dress has obtained “secondary meaning” in the marketplace; (2) the trade dress of the two competing products is confusingly similar; and (3) the appropriated features of the trade dress are primarily nonfunctional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade dress can include packaging, product designs, store décor, and even sales techniques (examples: décor of a chain of Mexican restaurants, adoption-simulation sales techniques for Cabbage Patch Kids). ‘‘Secondary meaning’’ means the primary significance of the trade dress in the minds of the public is to identify the product’s source rather than the product itself. Nonfunctionality is required for trade dress protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: When domain names function as marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain names are addresses on the Internet, but they do not act as marks in identifying the source of goods or services except when used as something other than merely an address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A domain name may become a trademark/service mark when it is used on the site’s home page or in advertising to identify the source of specific services (example: Google on google.com). When the ‘.com’ is part of the identity of the service (example: Amazon.com advertising), the domain name functions as a service mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Certification marks certify that products or services manufactured or provided by others have certain qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification marks are intended to be used by persons authorized by the certifier and will certify specific attributes (example: Vidalia for onions certifying yellow Granex type onions grown by authorized growers within the Vidalia production area). Certification marks differ from trademarks in that the owner of the mark does not use the goods/services directly but certifies standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective marks are used by members of a group or organization to identify the goods they produce or services they provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective marks identify membership-sourced goods or services (example: ILGU — International Ladies Garment Union). They function like trademarks for members’ offerings and are registerable and protectable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of distinctiveness and mark selection guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a hierarchy of marks, with the most distinctive marks being afforded a wider scope of protection: fanciful or arbitrary (most distinctive), then suggestive, then merely descriptive, and finally generic (not protectable). It is best to select a mark that is fanciful, arbitrary, or suggestive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fanciful: created solely as a mark with no other meaning (Xerox, Kodak). Arbitrary: common word applied in a non-descriptive way (Apple for computers). Suggestive: suggests qualities requiring imagination (Coppertone). Merely descriptive: immediately conveys product qualities and affords the narrowest protection; protectable only upon a showing of secondary meaning. Generic: common name of a class; never functions as a trademark (e.g., ‘computer software’). The more inherently distinctive the mark, the broader the protection and the easier registration and enforcement will be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary meaning requirement for merely descriptive marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A merely descriptive mark is protectable only upon a showing of a secondary meaning or distinctiveness — that the consumer accepts and recognizes the term as denoting only one source rather than merely describing the goods or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often consider: (1) the amount and manner of advertising, (2) the volume of sales, (3) the length and manner of the term’s use, and (4) the results of consumer surveys when deciding whether a term has acquired secondary meaning. Examples of merely descriptive marks found protectable only with secondary meaning: Chap-Stick, Hour after Hour deodorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-adoption investigation and searching requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the mark is selected but prior to its use, a thorough search should be undertaken to determine whether the mark is available for both use and federal registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search sources and methods recommended: USPTO federal register and pending applications (online at uspto.gov), Trademarkscan/Dialogue databases (federal and state files), private search firms (Thompson & Thompson, Dialog, Questel/Orbit, Micropatent, Corsearch), state trademark records, foreign trademark records (Canada, France, Germany, UK) if foreign use contemplated, and Internet/domain name searches (Network Solutions WOSIT, browser searches). Also check business directories (Big Book, Switchboard, Superpages, World Pages). Remember constructive notice from federal registrations; an abandoned registration may still reflect ongoing common-law rights. Searching thoroughly reduces risk of conflicting use and provides notice of existing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common misconceptions about mark rights and registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Common misconceptions that can mislead mark users: incorporation or assumed-name filings do not automatically give right to use a name as a mark; a person does not have an absolute right to use their own name as a trademark; state registration does not guarantee permissibility of use everywhere; abandoned or expired registrations may still correspond to ongoing common-law rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: do not rely solely on incorporation, state filings, or abandoned/expired USPTO records; conduct comprehensive searches and consider potential common-law users before adopting and using a mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration in the USPTO, use-in-commerce requirement, and benefits of federal registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is not required to establish rights in a mark (rights are based on use), but federal registration confers significant nationwide benefits even if actual use is geographically limited. A federal application can be filed based on a good faith intent to use in interstate commerce, but a registration will not issue until actual use in interstate commerce occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Trademark Act (15 U.S.C. §1127) definition of use in commerce: ‘The term “use in commerce” means that the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and not made merely to reserve a right in a mark. For purposes of this Act, a mark shall be deemed to be in use in commerce (1) on goods when (A) it is placed in any manner on the goods or their containers or the displays associated therewith or on the tags or labels affixed thereto…’ (text continues). Practical guidance: consider filing intent-to-use applications when appropriate, but be aware registration will not issue absent actual use; federal registration provides nationwide constructive notice and other enforcement advantages.
